points: Aeolian processes are the erosion, transport and deposition of material by wind.
Wind erosion is most effective in hot and cold deserts and on coasts, where loose, dry, fine material lies, vegetation is sparse and winds are strong.
Air is far less dense than water or ice, so wind can move only sand and finer particles, and mostly close to the ground.
Deflation: wind lifts and blows away loose, dry, fine particles (dust, silt and sand), lowering the land surface.
Abrasion (sandblasting): sand grains carried by the wind strike rock surfaces and wear them away. Abrasion is most effective within a metre or two of the ground, where most sand is carried.
Attrition: wind-blown grains collide with each other and with rock, becoming smaller, rounder and frosted.
Suspension: fine dust is carried high in the air, sometimes for thousands of kilometres in dust storms.
Saltation: sand grains bounce along the surface in short hops. Most wind-blown sand moves this way.
Surface creep: larger grains are pushed and rolled along by the impact of saltating grains.

Deflation hollow: a depression formed where deflation removes loose material down to the water table or to a resistant layer. The Qattara Depression, Egypt, lies below sea level and is attributed mainly to deflation down to the water table.
Desert pavement (reg): a surface of closely packed stones left after deflation has blown away the fine material between them. The stones protect the ground below from further deflation.
Ventifacts: stones with flat, polished faces and sharp edges, cut by sandblasting from the prevailing wind direction.
Diagram: plan of a deflation hollow; cross-section of a desert pavement.
Yardangs: long, streamlined ridges of rock lying parallel to the prevailing wind, separated by grooves abraded in softer rock.
Zeugens: tabular, flat-topped ridges where a hard cap rock overlies softer rock. They form where the rock layers are horizontal and the joints run across the wind.
Zeugen stages: 1. Abrasion cuts down along joints in the cap rock. 2. The soft rock beneath is undercut. 3. A flat-topped ridge remains.
Mushroom (pedestal) rocks: rock pillars undercut near the base by sandblasting, which is concentrated near the ground.
Mushroom rock stages: 1. A pillar of rock stands on the desert floor. 2. Sandblasting undercuts its base. 3. The top, above the zone of abrasion, stays wide, leaving a mushroom shape.
Diagram: plan of yardangs aligned with the wind; cross-sections of a zeugen and a mushroom rock.
Deposition occurs when wind speed drops or the wind meets an obstacle.
Desert landscapes: erg (sand sea), reg (stony desert) and hamada (bare rock). The Sahara Desert, North Africa, has all three.
Barchan dunes: crescent-shaped dunes with horns pointing downwind. They have a gentle windward slope and a steep slip face on the lee side, and migrate downwind.
Seif (linear) dunes: long ridges roughly parallel to the dominant wind, formed where winds blow from two directions.
Loess: fine wind-blown dust, often from the edges of former ice sheets or deserts, which forms very fertile soils. Example: the Loess Plateau of northern China.
Diagram: cross-section of a barchan dune showing the windward slope and slip face.

The Dust Bowl, Great Plains of the USA (including Oklahoma and Kansas), 1930s: bare, dry soil was blown away in huge dust storms, known as black blizzards (see the notes on Human interaction: mass movement for its causes).

In Ireland, the damp climate and vegetation cover limit wind erosion. The main aeolian landforms are coastal sand dunes (see the notes on Coastal processes, patterns and associated landforms (The Sea at Work)) and blowouts where dune vegetation is damaged (see the notes on Human interaction: coastal processes (The Sea at Work)).

keyTerms.definition: The erosion, transport and deposition of material by wind.

The transport of sand grains by short bouncing hops along the surface.
A surface of closely packed stones left after wind has removed the fine material between them.

factCards.term: Wind erosion: where it works best, and why it is weaker than water
factCards.definition: In hot and cold deserts, such as the Sahara, and on coasts, with loose, dry, fine material, sparse vegetation and strong winds. Air is far less dense than water or ice, so wind moves only sand and finer particles, mostly near the ground.

factCards.term: Wind erosion: three processes and what each does
factCards.definition: Deflation: wind lifts and blows away loose, dry, fine particles, lowering the surface. Abrasion (sandblasting): wind-blown sand wears rock away, mostly within a metre or two of the ground. Attrition: grains collide and become smaller, rounder and frosted.

Suspension: fine dust is carried high, sometimes thousands of kilometres in dust storms. Saltation: sand grains bounce along in short hops; most sand moves this way. Surface creep: larger grains are pushed and rolled along by the impact of saltating grains.

factCards.term: Mushroom (pedestal) rock: how it forms, in stages
factCards.definition: First, a pillar of rock stands on the desert floor; then sandblasting, which is concentrated near the ground, undercuts its base; finally the top, above the zone of abrasion, stays wide, leaving a mushroom shape.

factCards.term: Zeugen: how it forms, in stages
factCards.definition: Where horizontal layers of hard cap rock lie over softer rock and joints run across the wind: first, abrasion cuts down along joints in the cap rock; then the soft rock beneath is undercut; finally a flat-topped ridge is left.

factCards.term: Deflation hollow: how it forms, with an example
factCards.definition: Deflation removes loose material until it reaches the water table or a resistant layer, leaving a depression. The Qattara Depression, Egypt, below sea level, is attributed mainly to deflation down to the water table.

factCards.term: Desert landscapes: erg, reg and hamada
factCards.definition: Erg: a sand sea. Reg: stony desert. Hamada: bare rock. The Sahara Desert, North Africa, has all three.

factCards.term: Barchan vs seif dunes: shape and the winds that form them
factCards.definition: Barchan: crescent-shaped, horns pointing downwind, gentle windward slope and steep slip face on the lee side; it migrates downwind. Seif (linear): a long ridge roughly parallel to the dominant wind, formed where winds blow from two directions.

factCards.term: Dust Bowl: where and when it happened, and what the wind did
factCards.definition: On the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, in the 1930s, bare, dry soil was blown away in huge dust storms, known as black blizzards.

questions.prompt: Examine the processes of erosion by wind and explain the formation of one landform of wind erosion.
questions.model: Processes: deflation lifts loose, dry, fine particles and lowers the surface; abrasion, by sand grains carried within a metre or two of the ground, wears rock surfaces; attrition makes wind-blown grains smaller and rounder. Transport: suspension carries fine dust high in the air; saltation moves most sand in short hops; surface creep rolls larger grains. Landform: a mushroom rock. 1. A rock pillar stands on the desert floor. 2. Sandblasting, concentrated near the ground, undercuts its base. 3. The top, above the zone of abrasion, stays wide, leaving a mushroom shape. Diagram: labelled sketch of the pillar with the undercut base and the wider top.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between deflation and abrasion as processes of wind erosion.
questions.model: Deflation is the lifting and blowing away of loose, dry, fine particles such as dust, silt and sand, which lowers the land surface. Abrasion is the wearing away of rock surfaces by sand grains carried by the wind, which strike the rock, and is most effective within a metre or two of the ground. Deflation removes material; abrasion wears rock down by impact.
